defaults.permitted_development: Across Kent, a wraparound extension only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A when read together. The combined footprint, leftover garden and mass at the rear corner are often what force the scheme into a full application.

rules.height_rules: Across Kent, single-storey wraparounds still need to stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can bite close to a boundary. The lower the side arm reads, the safer the design usually is.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to satisfy the normal rear-extension depth rules and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound cannot borrow generosity from one side of the design to excuse excess on the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Kent, neighbour impact is usually judged at the side boundary and rear corner together. A scheme that looks acceptable in plan can still feel overbearing once those two faces are read as one mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof quiet and subordinate. The more the roof wraps around as one bulky form, the harder it is to argue that the work remains a modest householder addition.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the side-and-rear combination reads as one coherent addition rather than an oversized add-on.

rules.permitted_development: The wraparound fallback is narrow: both the side return and the rear projection have to satisfy Class A as one combined proposal. In Ashford, the side arm is usually the limiting piece because tight plot width makes the whole wraparound read much larger than the plan suggests.

rules.height_rules: For height, the familiar Class A envelope still applies, but the side arm is usually the sensitive part because of the 3m eaves rule close to a boundary. In Ashford, the roof usually needs most restraint over the side arm, where the closeness of the boundary amplifies every bit of bulk.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact on a wraparound is rarely just about depth; the side relationship and the rear-corner mass often create the real pressure point. In Ashford, tight boundaries mean the wraparound has to be judged as a sequence of impacts, not as one depth figure.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. On exposed coastal sites, roof profile, external finish and visual impact can carry more weight than on a routine suburban plot.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually tightens scrutiny on wraparounds because the side return and turning corner can alter character more than their footprint suggests.
restrictions.listed_building: If the house is listed, a wraparound should be approached as heritage work, with listed building consent usually needed for any extension affecting character.
restrictions.article4_notes: Because Article 4 controls operate within this authority, the wraparound route needs a property-specific check before it is treated as available.
